column1: # suites.tsv - what each lane runs, and the desktop each suite needs.
# Until this file existed, the answer to "what does the kde lane run" was to read
# 3365 lines of .github/workflows/ci.yml and hold thirty steps in your head. The
# lanes genuinely differ -- that is the point of having ten of them -- but the
# difference was an emergent property of a YAML file rather than something a
# reader could see, and the difference that was there by accident looked exactly
# like the difference that was there on purpose.
# So the divergence is declared. `themescheme` runs on GTK lanes and not on Qt
# ones because WebKitGTK's prefers-color-scheme follows the theme's *name*; that
# is a fact worth writing down once, in the place that decides it, instead of
# being visible only as a step that is present in one job and absent in another.
# `lane` is a lane key. `<lane>:<phase>` names one pass of a lane that runs its
# list more than once: linux-engines swaps its engine packages and runs the same
# suites again, and until now the two halves filed their rows under one name and
# neither was attributable. Everything left of the colon is what reaches
# $NT_LANE, so cases.tsv and the grid never see a phase.
# `suite` is the name, and it is four things at once: step.sh's --log, the
# $NT_SUITE the harness files rows under, the heading in the job log, and the row
# in the timing table. Unique per lane. A row whose suite column is `*` is the
# `setup` is space-separated directives from a closed vocabulary, listed in
# test/run.sh. An unknown directive is an error and not a shrug: a typo that is
# silently ignored is a suite running without the display it asked for.
# `command` is argv, split on whitespace and run through test/step.sh. Because it
# is argv and not a shell fragment, a suite that needs a variable in its
# environment spells it with env(1) in this column, and there is no `env=`
# directive to specify, test and explain.
# `display=metacity gtk` is true of fourteen gjs rows and would be written
# fourteen times. The `*` row says it once and every suite row on that lane
# merges over it, so what is left in a row is only what makes that row different
# -- which is the whole reason to read one.
# File order is run order. That matters more here than it did in YAML, where the
# step list was the order and could not be anything else: selftest stays first on
# the lanes that run it, because a broken reporter makes every reading behind it
# unreadable and that is worth finding out first.
# Provisioning is not a suite. apt, brew, sysctl, setup-zig, docker login, the
# engine-removal guards, anything reading a secret and anything with a ${{ }} in
# it stays in the workflow, which is the thing that owns the machine. So does
# every `uses:` step, and the sheet and upload steps at the end of each lane --
# those name per-lane picture directories with human captions and there is
# Four lanes have no rows here at all, and should not. bsd, kde-live, wayland and
# macos-netinstall each run one command -- netinstall/test/run.sh, or qtkde.sh --
# inside a VM action or a container pull. netinstall has a runner of its own and
# it is better at that job than this one would be. This is the runner for the
# test/ tree, and four lanes running neither is the honest answer; it is the same
# A lane moves onto this file one suite at a time. `run.sh <lane> a b c` runs
# only the rows it names, so a row that exists here and is not yet named by the
# workflow does not run, and a step the workflow still spells by hand is not
# duplicated. The rows below are the twenty steps that were already one-liners
# through step.sh -- the safest thing to move first, and the set whose arithmetic
# this runner has to get right before anything harder is put through it.
# The leashes are the `timeout-minutes` those steps carried, in seconds. They
# were a ceiling GitHub enforced per step; a lane is fewer steps now, so the leash
# a row declares is the one that suite has. That is also why test/step.sh grew a
# watchdog: on macOS there is no timeout(1), and a declared leash with nothing
# behind it is the failure this project has a name for.
